item.title: Instant gratification is ruining our lives – and for me it started with my CD player’s shuffle button | Adrian Chiles
item.description: Not even a compelling TV drama can stop me from staring at my phone. But this urge started 40 years ago, with what was at first presented as a useful feature I blame the shuffle button. That’s what started me on the long road to a thoroughly scattered mind – generally unable to focus on anything for more than a few minutes or even seconds. I was always a bit like this, hence an ADHD diagnosis in later life. But back in the day I still managed to read a lot of books, watch long films and listen to whole records at one sitting. Now? item.description: Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passion Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work. But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood. item.title: The unexpected power of fleeting friendships
item.description: From Aristotle on, we’ve learned to see long-lasting relationships as more valuable. But what does that leave out? In Russian, a poputchik is a stranger you meet on a journey who you end up confessing everything to because you know you’ll never see them again. Like the English “fellow traveller”, poputchik was repurposed to describe Marxist sympathisers, but the original meaning intrigues me most. The idea that we might safely unburden ourselves to strangers, or have their secrets bestowed upon us, is deeply embedded in Russian culture. It’s there in Leo Tolstoy’s The Kreutzer Sonata: as the windows tremble and the tundra passes in a hypnotic blur, Pozdnyshev tells his life story of marriage, betrayal and murder.
